title: BUG #19078: Segfaults in tts_minimal_store_tuple() following pg_upgrade
body: We are encountering intermittent PostgreSQL backend segfaults in tts_minimal_store_tuple() after upgrading clusters from PostgreSQL 17 to PostgreSQL 18 with pg_upgradecluster --method link on Debian 13. The affected SELECT and UPDATE queries usually succeed but can crash across multiple physical hosts, with frequency depending on cluster size and load. Disabling huge pages and JIT, changing checkpoint and I/O settings, reindexing, repacking affected tables, and running pg_amcheck did not stop the crashes. I have just disabled enable_hashagg for some affected queries, but do not yet know whether that prevents them.

symptoms_visible: After upgrading from PostgreSQL 17 to 18, my SELECT and UPDATE workloads intermittently terminate backends with signal 11 and a stack trace involving tts_minimal_store_tuple().
The same queries usually finish successfully, and the crashes occur on multiple physical hosts despite reindexing, pg_repack, pg_amcheck, and several configuration changes.
N0.label: N0 intermittent post-upgrade HashAgg crash reported

symptoms_visible: In several days of A/B testing, the affected hash-aggregation queries crashed when hash aggregation was enabled, while disabling enable_hashagg stopped all crashes in that subset.
N1.label: N1 HashAgg dependency confirmed

symptoms_visible: In the existing crash dump, I see perhash->hashiter->end equal to 43, hashtable->hashtab->size equal to 16, and the invalid firstTuple value 0x1b.
N2.label: N2 inconsistent HashAgg state values captured

symptoms_visible: With assertions enabled and my original data and queries, the first diagnostic patch triggers its assertions immediately.
With the second candidate patch, the same tests complete without assertions or crashes.
N3.label: N3 candidate HashAgg correction verified

symptoms_visible: The build with the HashAgg correction no longer crashes under my original assertion-enabled tests, but I have not yet completed longer-term monitoring on production.
N_terminal.label: N_terminal fix pushed after candidate verification

question_patterns: How sure are you that these crashes stop when enable_hashagg is off?
Can you A/B test the affected queries with hash aggregation enabled and disabled and report whether either configuration still crashes?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I am sure for the subset of queries that uses hash aggregation. I A/B tested them over a few days, and enable_hashagg=off stopped all of those crashes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same tts_minimal_store_tuple crash still occurs at the same rate with enable_hashagg=off.
Disabling hash aggregation greatly reduces the crashes, but I saw one similar crash during the test window.

edges.comment: Thread c0 and c3, describing the reporter's production query subset: Jeff Davis asks whether HashAgg is genuinely required, and the reporter supplies the multi-day A/B result. The separately reproduced partition-pruning crash discussed in c1-c8 is not folded into this HashAgg causal chain.

question_patterns: Can you inspect the existing core dump and report the suspicious bounds and pointer values around the crash?
What values do the relevant end, size, and firstTuple fields have in the failing aggregate state?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: In the dump I get perhash->hashiter->end=43 and hashtable->hashtab->size=16. Their difference is 0x1b, which is also the suspicious firstTuple value I was looking at.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The end value is below the table size, and firstTuple is a normally aligned allocated address.
I get different absolute values, but the end value is still larger than the table size and the invalid pointer matches their difference.

edges.comment: Thread c12-c14 on the reporter's original HashAgg core dump: the reporter reads raw structure values after maintainers request more debugging. The conclusion that an iterator is being used with the wrong hash table remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can you build PostgreSQL with assertions, apply the first attached diagnostic patch, and run your original data and queries?
Please test the assertion-enabled diagnostic build and tell me whether an assertion fires.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested with assertions and my original data and queries. With the first patch, the assertions trigger as soon as I run the tests.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The diagnostic assertions never trigger even after the workload crashes again.

question_patterns: Can you apply the second candidate patch to the assertion-enabled build and rerun the same workload?
Please test the candidate patched build with your original data and queries and report whether it still asserts or crashes.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With the second patch there are no issues and no more crashing. I tested it with assertions and the original data and queries, although I still need longer production monitoring to be 100% sure.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The second patched build still triggers the same assertion and segfaults with my original workload.
The second patched build passes the same tests, but I have only run it for a shorter period and still need production monitoring.

edges.comment: Thread c14-c20 on the reporter's own original data and queries. The reporter executes two pre-landing build measurements: the diagnostic assertion patch fails immediately, while the candidate correction survives the same assertion-enabled workload. These are measurements rather than persistent production changes.

solution.intent: Correct the HashAgg grouping-sets transition so the iterator for the newly selected grouping set is reset against that same set's hash table, then ship the correction on the affected PostgreSQL branch and have the reporter verify a build containing it.
solution.concrete_example: After select_current_set changes aggstate->current_set and perhash, reset perhash->hashiter with perhash->hashtable rather than the stale hash table from the previous grouping set. The correction was pushed for PostgreSQL 18 after the reporter's assertion-enabled candidate build stopped crashing.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the raw iterator end, table size, invalid pointer, assertion result, and candidate-build outcome. David Rowley inferred from those values and source inspection that nodeAgg.c changed to the next grouping set and its perhash iterator but passed the previous hash table to ResetTupleHashIterator. The source-level mismatch and its distinction from the separately fixed partition-pruning/EPQ crash are engineer conclusions.

edges.comment: Thread c15-c22: David Rowley identifies the mismatched hash table and iterator, constructs a grouping-sets reproducer, supplies the corrective patch, and pushes it after the reporter's successful candidate test and Jeff Davis's review. The reporter explicitly still wanted production monitoring, so the terminal state records technical verification and landing without inventing a later production or packaged-release retest.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: during a HashAgg grouping-sets transition, PostgreSQL reset the newly selected set's tuple-hash iterator using the previous set's hash table, allowing iteration beyond the bucket array and producing the invalid firstTuple access.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: crashes depend on HashAgg, hashiter->end exceeds the hash-table size in the dump, the diagnostic assertion fires, and the candidate corrected build survives the reporter's original workload.
The fix must pair perhash->hashiter with the current perhash->hashtable when resetting the iterator; enable_hashagg=off may be offered only as a temporary crash-avoidance measure.
Must not conflate this HashAgg defect with the separately reproduced partition-pruning/EPQ crash; the earlier pruning patch was explicitly reported not to address tts_minimal_store_tuple().
Must ask the reporter to verify a build containing the shipped correction and complete production monitoring before declaring the issue fully resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced PostgreSQL operator who manages very large, highly concurrent clusters and can build PostgreSQL from source, use GDB, inspect core-dump structures, enable assertions, and run controlled A/B workload tests, but is unfamiliar with PostgreSQL executor internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, cooperative, and evidence-driven; provides exact configuration and debugger values, follows build-and-test instructions, separates query classes when prompted, and is cautious about claiming resolution before production monitoring.
